summary:
SphereX is a free website that lets anyone watch the infrared sky change. NASA's SPHEREx telescope maps the whole sky every six months in 102 infrared colours, but its photos sit in an expert archive that can't play them over time.

With SphereX, you search a star by name, by coordinates, or by clicking the sky. It finds every SPHEREx photo of that spot live from NASA/IPAC IRSA, lines them up and plays them as a flipbook. Changes are marked in colour, and each one gets a plain-language verdict checked against ESA's Gaia catalogue, such as "Known moving star: Barnard's Star". Clicking any star shows its colour fingerprint, with water, methane, CO₂ and CO bands marked.

This matters because things that move across the sky in months are our closest neighbours. Cold brown dwarfs, or a hidden "Planet X", are nearly invisible to Gaia but glow in infrared. SphereX turns SPHEREx's data into a tool that anyone can use to look for them.
details:
SphereX is a free website that turns NASA's SPHEREx data into a time-lapse of the infrared sky. You search a star by name or coordinates, or click the all-sky map. SphereX finds every SPHEREx photo of that spot live from NASA/IPAC IRSA (358 photos of Barnard's Star in about 2 seconds), lines them up and plays them as a flipbook. Changes are marked in colour, and each one gets a plain-language verdict checked against ESA's Gaia catalogue, such as "Known moving star: Barnard's Star, motion consistent with Gaia, seen in 6 of 6 detectors". Clicking any star shows its colour fingerprint, with water, methane, CO2 and CO bands marked.

How it works: a Python server on Google Cloud Run reads only the rows it needs from each 65 MB photo in NASA's public cloud storage, about 8 KB per photo. It cleans each cut-out, aligns it north-up and streams it to the browser, which compares the photos on the GPU. To keep it honest, we only compare photos taken in the same colours, mark only changes well above the measured noise, and require changes to appear in several detectors. On an ordinary patch of sky this cut false alarms from 5 to 0.

Why it matters: objects that move across the sky in months are our closest neighbours. Cold brown dwarfs, or a hidden "Planet X", are nearly invisible to Gaia but glow in infrared. SphereX lets anyone explore SPHEREx data and look for them. We want to make exploring space via SPHEREx an accessible experience for all. We want to push new discoveries to their limit.

Tools: Python, FastAPI, Astropy, NumPy, SciPy, JavaScript, WebGL2, Aladin Lite, Google Cloud Run and GitHub Pages. Everything is free to use and to host.
